nameStory: The Silver Spotted Anemone gets its name from the distinctive silvery-white spots that dot its column like scattered coins. These metallic-looking markings shine against the anemone's darker base color, making it easy to spot among other sea anemones in New England tide pools.
description: The Silver Spotted Anemone is a chunky, barrel-shaped sea anemone that looks like a living flower when its tentacles are extended. It typically grows 2-4 inches across and about 3 inches tall, with a sturdy column (body) topped by a crown of short, thick tentacles. When disturbed, it can quickly pull in its tentacles and close up into a dome-shaped blob that's surprisingly firm to the touch.

idTips.label: Silver spots on column
idTips.description: Look for distinctive silvery-white or pale spots scattered across the dark brown to olive-green body column - they feel smooth and slightly raised when gently touched

idTips.label: Thick, short tentacles
idTips.description: The tentacles are noticeably chunky and stubby compared to other anemones, feeling firm and slightly sticky when they touch your finger

idTips.label: Barrel-shaped body
idTips.description: The column is wider than it is tall, giving it a squat, robust appearance that feels solid and muscular when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Dark base coloration
idTips.description: The background color ranges from deep brown to olive-green or reddish-brown, providing contrast for the silver spots

idTips.label: Firm attachment
idTips.description: Strongly attached to rocks and very difficult to dislodge without damage - much more firmly stuck than most other anemones

habitat: Found in rocky intertidal zones along New England's coast, particularly in the mid to low tide areas where they attach firmly to granite and other hard surfaces. They prefer somewhat sheltered spots in tide pools or crevices where they won't be pounded by the heaviest waves. Often found alongside mussels, barnacles, and other sea anemones like the Northern Red Anemone.

seasonality.spring: Most active as warmer water returns, with tentacles frequently extended for feeding. Good time to observe feeding behavior as they capture small crustaceans and fish.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with tentacles often fully displayed. Colors are most vibrant, and the silver spots are easiest to see against the darker column.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may begin retracting more frequently as water temperatures drop. Silver spots remain clearly visible on the exposed column.
seasonality.winter: Often found contracted into a tight dome shape during low tides. The silver spots are still visible but the anemone is less responsive to gentle touch.

funFact: Silver Spotted Anemones can live for over 60 years and some individuals may be older than the person observing them - that chunky little tide pool creature could have been feeding in the same spot since the 1960s!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with Northern Red Anemones, but the silver spots are a dead giveaway - no other New England anemone has these metallic markings. Remember: 'Silver spots = Silver Spotted' - it's really that simple!
compareHints: Since it's the only Aulactinia species in New England, compare it with other common tide pool anemones in the Actiniidae family. Unlike the Northern Red Anemone which is taller and lacks spots, or the Frilled Anemone with its distinctive wavy column edge, the Silver Spotted Anemone's combination of squat shape and metallic spots makes it unmistakable. It's also much more firmly attached than most other local anemone species.
